questions.q: What two questions does the summary suggest asking about each possession at home?
a: When did I last use this, and how much do I like it?
How much did this cost, and could I resell it?
Would a guest notice this, and does it match the room?
Who gave me this, and am I obliged to keep it?
questions.why: Lesson 1 recommends picking up every item and asking when you last used it and how much you like it.

questions.q: Besides filling the house, what does the summary say clutter does?
a: It fills your mind and distracts you from what matters
It makes family members argue more often
It drains your energy through extra cleaning
It lowers the value of the home over time
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that a cluttered space also clutters the mind, leaving less room for important things.

questions.q: How does Rubin recommend reacting when her daughter spills nail polish on the carpet?
a: Calmly have the child look up how to remove the stain
Clean it up herself without saying anything
Send the child to her room for the evening
Replace the carpet and split the cost
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes underreacting: she stayed calm, and her daughter found a cleaning method and learned a skill.

questions.q: Where should you display the possessions you value most?
a: Where you can see them every day
Stored safely out of direct sunlight
In a locked drawer for protection
Grouped together in the least used room
questions.why: Lesson 1 advises keeping the possessions you care about most in plain sight, such as family photos on a main wall.

questions.q: What does the summary say can start a friendship with a neighbor?
a: Small gestures like sharing muffins or borrowing sugar
Inviting the whole street to a large party
Joining a formal neighborhood committee
Exchanging phone numbers during a meeting
questions.why: Lesson 3 says great friendships often begin with simple exchanges such as baked goods or a borrowed cup of sugar.
